item.title: Far-right broadcaster ON switched off over licensing breaches
item.description:
Far-right broadcaster ON switched off over licensing breaches

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Culture minister Rianne Letschert has confirmed that she intends to take far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland off the airwaves after the media regulator asked her to withdraw its licence.

Letschert said the decision was the “most serious means at my disposal” and followed a series of breaches of broadcasting rules since ON started showing programmes on the Dutch public networks in 2022.

“There are clear rules for broadcasters that want to make programmes with public money,” the minister said. ”And if you repeatedly fail to abide by them, there comes a point where it has to stop.”

The breaking point was a panel discussion posted on ON’s YouTube channel in July that featured a clip from a speech by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler in which he fulminated against the ”rootless international clique”, referring to the Jews.

Panellists, including editor-in-chief Joost Niemöller, agreed with a proposition that the “cosmopolitan elite” was “essentially hostile” to ordinary people, though they also rejected Hitler’s anti-Semitism.

Vlemmix called the decision a “very worrying day for Dutch public broadcasting” and said he would fight for “the interests of everyone who welcomes our views, but also public broadcasting and the views of the right in general.”

Regulator call

Letschert had previously rejected demands to take ON off the air, arguing that as a government minister she could not interfere in its editorial line.

Her legal position changed when the media regulator CvdM wrote to her last week telling her that ON was not fulfilling its obligations under Dutch broadcasting law.

The NPO, which is responsible for the three Dutch public TV channels, also asked the minister to intervene because ON was not prepared to work as a partner organisation.

The broadcasting ombudsman has reprimanded the channel several times for disseminating untrue information and mixing fact with opinion.

ON has also been fined twice in the last year by the media regulator, once for breaching conflict of interest rules and once for breaching its own editorial code.

Letschert said those three reasons were enough for her to pull ON’s licence, though the broadcaster will not be taken off the air immediately because it has the right to appeal against her decision.

Rules of freedom

“The Netherlands is a democratic state that observes the rule of law. That obliges us to take great care with the decisions we make,” she said. “Ongehoord Nederland will therefore have the opportunity to respond to my proposal and I will consider that response carefully before I make a final decision.

“A free public broadcasting system should have space for difference, debate and for views that clash and sometimes cause offence. But that freedom is only strong if everyone observes the rules that protect it.”

item.title: ASML begins building new 20,000-workplace Eindhoven campus
item.description:
ASML begins building new 20,000-workplace Eindhoven campus

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Chip machinery maker ASML has begun building a second industrial campus in Eindhoven, with the first buildings due to open in 2029.

The site will be developed in phases and could eventually cover 350,000 square metres, with room for up to 20,000 workplaces, the company said.

Prime minister Rob Jetten attended a ceremony at the site on Tuesday at Brainport Industries Campus North, close to Eindhoven Airport and the A58 motorway.

The first phase will house at least 3,000 staff and combine production, logistics and offices in one location. Most of those posts will be filled by teams moving from ASML’s existing locations rather than new hires, and the company said later phases would depend on future demand for its machines.

Growing demand
“The growing global demand from the semiconductor industry requires continuous investments,” chief executive Christophe Fouquet said in a statement. “BIC North provides the space and flexibility we need to continue innovating and supporting our customers around the world.”

The new campus will include what ASML calls a “flow factory”, a production line for its chip lithography machines modelled on methods used in the car and aircraft industries.

Eindhoven city council approved the zoning plan for the site in March, after the government pledged €2.5 billion in 2024 for housing, roads, education and power grid upgrades in the region to persuade the company to expand in the Netherlands rather than abroad.

ASML’s headquarters are in nearby Veldhoven. In January it announced 1,700 job cuts, mostly in the Netherlands, despite a record year.

item.title: Mind the gap: how 30% ruling changes may affect your paycheck
item.description:
Partner content

Mind the gap: how 30% ruling changes may affect your paycheck

September 8, 2026

If you are one of those clever people who spent years studying abroad and is now contributing skills to the Dutch economy, there’s good and bad news.

Some economists in the Netherlands have raised alarm bells at the drop in highly-skilled migrants since the failed “hard right” government in 2023. The first international scientists have landed in the Netherlands as the result of a new “tulip” fund to support top thinkers.

But at the same time, the country is winding back a ruling to compensate some temporary highly-skilled workers for their costs, and it will in future be restricted to people with even higher salaries.

From next year, for new highly-skilled migrants and everyone who arrived after January 1, 2024, the 30% ruling for people with rare skills will be cut to 27%. This means that for five years, the first 27% of their salary will be paid untaxed – an incentive to make this high-tax country more attractive and compensate top international talent for costs such as expensive housing.

“This will make a difference of between €50 and €100 a month for most of the people we help,” said a tax adviser for Blue Umbrella. “One more dinner at home each month, perhaps, but it is still money.”

The tax break, which has strict conditions and must be applied for by the employer, will also only be valid for salaries from just over €50,000 from 2027, or for masters students under 30, earning from around € 38,000. This is a slight rise from the current levels.

It is also limited at the top end to what is known as the Balkenendenorm, the top salary for civil servants and quango employees – €262,000 this year. There are around 100,000 people nationally with the “expat” ruling for skills that cannot be found locally and most Blue Umbrella clients and internationals, of course, earn nothing like this amount.

“Typically, it’s around €60,000 to €80,000,” says the Blue Umbrella adviser, who points out that this may be a family’s single salary after an international move. “Every month, the expat ruling might save €500 on the usual tax rate. And they will lose an extra 3%.”

While there is sometimes criticism of highly-skilled migrants in Dutch media for living in local housing, Blue Umbrella points out that these people are vital for the economy.

“Fewer of them are coming to the Netherlands in general because the mood is one where we say: no migrants,” he said. “But we need highly-skilled migrants. Companies are closing in the games industry and IT specialists are going to other countries that try to attract them, like Portugal.”

The tax climate is less conducive to starting a business too, he added, meaning that entrepreneurs may be less likely to choose the Netherlands. But Blue Umbrella is hopeful that there will be a greater realisation that this small country is competing for global talent.

“We are a knowledge economy, we are known for technology and trading, and you need smart people,” he said. “There’s a battle going on around the world because other countries want them too. We are known for our schools and education, the cyber war is coming, and this should be a moment of change.”

Find out more about your personal tax situation and the 27% ruling by contacting Blue Umbrella.

item.title: IND pays out €99m in seven months for missing asylum deadlines
item.description:
IND pays out €99m in seven months for missing asylum deadlines

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The immigration service IND paid out around €99 million in court-ordered penalties in the first seven months of this year for failing to decide on residency and asylum applications on time, already exceeding the record €79 million it paid in the whole of 2025.

Asylum minister Bart van den Brink revealed the figures in a written response to requests from MPs.

The IND paid €36.8 million in penalties in 2024 and €79 million in 2025, when the average waiting time for an asylum decision reached 67 weeks. The 2026 total is running at about €14 million a month, against €6.6 million a month last year.

The answers also show the number of individual payments above €3,000 has risen from 858 in 2023 to 6,368 in 2025. By July 2 this year the IND had already made 5,442 such payments.

How the penalties work
The IND is required by law to decide on an application within six months. If it misses the deadline, the applicant can ask a court to set a new one, and the court can attach a daily penalty if that deadline is also missed.

Courts normally set the penalty at €100 a day up to a maximum of €15,000, rising to €250 a day and a €37,500 cap where a “strong incentive” is needed, according to the minister’s answers. Applicants can go back to court as often as they like for as long as no decision has been taken, so the totals in individual cases can build up over time.

Between the start of 2024 and May 11 this year, 143,190 people filed an appeal against a late decision, and 16,570 of them won two or more times, the minister said.

By July 29, courts had ordered the IND to pay a total of more than €80,000 to 46 individuals for failing to decide on their applications, and nine people received over €100,000.

Abolishing penalties 
Boomsma, who submitted the questions, told the Telegraaf the system was “completely bankrupt”, with court rulings making decisions ever harder to reach and taxpayers then paying for the resulting delays.

The IND has called for the penalties to be scrapped, saying they do nothing to speed up decisions and that dealing with the court cases takes staff away from processing applications.

An amendment abolishing court-imposed penalties in immigration cases, tabled by the orthodox Protestant SGP and JA21, was passed by the lower house of parliament in June as part of a wider bill on the detention of foreign nationals. The bill is now before the senate, which rejected the previous asylum emergency measures law containing the same measure in April.

Van den Brink said no date has been set for the senate debate and he could not estimate how much more the IND would have to pay before any abolition took effect. He also declined to forecast the total for 2026.

A previous attempt to scrap the penalties was struck down by the Council of State in 2022 as a breach of EU law, and refugee organisation VluchtelingenWerk has told MPs it considers the new amendment unlawful on the same grounds.

item.title: Dutch children’s literacy falls further behind European average
item.description:
Dutch children’s literacy falls further behind European average

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Nearly four in 10 Dutch children are at risk of leaving school with a low level of literacy, according to an international study that shows a steep decline in educational performance across Europe.

The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), carried out every three years in more than 90 countries, shows the Netherlands has fallen behind the European average over the past decade.

Dutch children still outperform their peers in most European countries in maths and science, where the figures show a less pronounced downward trend. In science they have dropped to the average level for the 23 nations in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) used for long-term comparisons.

The figures, which compare educational performance in 91 countries altogether, show a general worldwide decline in literacy standards since 2015, but the picture is especially stark in the Netherlands.

Some 39% of 15-year-olds had a reading level deemed inadequate to function in society, up from 33% the last time the report was compiled in 2022.

The points score used to grade performance has fallen from 503 in 2015 to 441 last year, including an 18-point drop between 2022 and 2025.

Three years behind

A drop of 20 points is seen as the equivalent of falling a year behind in educational development, meaning today’s 15-year-olds are learning at the same level as 12-year-olds a decade ago.

The 14 European countries which took part in the study – 13 EU nations plus the UK – had an average score of 464, with Ireland and Latvia topping the table. Singapore topped the global rankings with 535, followed by China.

Researchers speculated last time that school closures during the pandemic might be responsible for the decline in performance, but the continuing trend since the end of lockdown has forced them to consider that they may have overestimated the impact.

The growing use of digital technology such as smartphones, social media and AI may also be holding back the development of children’s reading skills, the researchers say.

Digital media

In a paper published last year they said children’s performance in maths, sense of belonging at school and overall life satisfaction were lower if they spent more time on their smartphones and called for more support for families to manage digital leisure time out of school.

The figures for science show Dutch students’ performance fell by three points to 485, one point lower than the OECD average, while in maths the Netherlands is still above the average despite dropping 10 points to 483.

Junior education minister Judith Thielen promised earlier this year to come up with an action plan in the autumn to tackle low literacy.

“It is my ambition to stop the downward trend and turn it around,” she said. “I want to see better results in three years’ time.”

item.title: Rutte: coronavirus curfew and school closures were “unavoidable”
item.description:
Rutte: coronavirus curfew and school closures were “unavoidable”

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Former prime minister Mark Rutte has defended the nationwide curfew imposed during the coronavirus lockdown, insisting it was “unavoidable”.

Giving evidence to the parliamentary inquiry into the government’s pandemic response, Rutte said there was “no alternative” to the drastic measure, which was in force for three months until the end of 2021.

Earlier witnesses including Hubert Bruls, the chair of the group of regional safety boards that were responsible for enforcing the lockdown rules, questioned whether the curfew was effective and said the government had failed to explain why it was necessary.

Riots broke out in several towns and cities during protests against the curfew, while in a poll by RTL this year 35% of people named it as the “most severe” of all the pandemic restrictions.

But Rutte said the curfew and other unpopular measures, such as shutting the schools, were essential to keep infections down and stop the health service reaching the “code black” crisis point.

He also defended the decision to close schools for a third time in December 2021 as the delta variant spread from the UK, after the education minister in his cabinet, Arie Slob, earlier said he was against the shutdown.

Delta variant

“The Delta variant meant that we had to take lockdown measures from October and November,” Rutte said.

“Then the Omicron variant appeared and all we knew was that it was highly infections. If it had been as debilitating as the Delta variant, code black would have been inevitable.”

Rutte also said he clashed with health minister Hugo de Jonge over vaccination policy. He was willing to set an example as prime minister by taking the jab, but it should be a matter of individual choice, while De Jonge believed the government should press people to take responsibility.

Rutte added that strict rules such as curfews would not have been needed if everyone had stuck to the basic rules announced at the start of the pandemic in March 2020.

“If everyone had said: I’ll keep to the one and a half metre rule, sneeze into my elbow, not shake hands and ventilate enough, then in theory we wouldn’t have had to take those measures,” he said.

item.title: Cabinet considers visa blocks for Russian athletes
item.description:
Cabinet considers visa blocks for Russian athletes

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch cabinet will do everything it can to prevent athletes from competing under the Russian flag at international sporting events, including the upcoming 2030 winter games in Heerenveen, sports minister Mirjam Sterk has said.

She told De Telegraaf that the government is actively lobbying the International Olympic Committee to reverse its decision to readmit Russian athletes, which it made this summer, clearing the way for the 2028 summer games in Los Angeles.

Russians were suspended in 2023 after the Putin regime began using sports bodies from occupied Ukrainian territories.

The cabinet’s stance would have consequences for the 2030 winter games at Thialf in Heerenveen, which will be the first Olympic competition on Dutch soil since 1928.

Asked what would happen if Russian skaters qualified to race there, Sterk told the paper: “You would have to look at what that means for the visas.”

“The cabinet considers the participation of Russian and Belarusian athletes and teams under their own flag and national symbols at sporting events in the Netherlands undesirable and will do everything within its power to prevent it,” she said. “That applies to individual athletes, national teams and club teams from both countries.”

Pressure on IOC funding
The Netherlands is one of nine EU countries, led by Estonia, that asked the European Commission in July to cut the IOC and other federations that readmit Russia out of Erasmus+ and other EU funding programmes.

Sterk said the primary responsibility lies with the sports federations, but that the Netherlands is raising the issue with them directly. “Russia also uses this to make political statements,” she said.

D66 MP Hanneke van der Werf backed the minister but said the message should have been made “much more emphatically and more widely” at the time. “Sport is not separate from reality when a regime deliberately uses it for political ends,” she told the Telegraaf.

item.title: Culture minister to decide on future of far-right broadcaster ON
item.description:
Culture minister to decide on future of far-right broadcaster ON

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Culture minister Rianne Letschert is under pressure to pull the plug on far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON) when she meets director-general Peter Vlemmix later on Tuesday.

The channel has been repeatedly criticised for breaching journalistic and ethical standards, most recently in an item that used footage of a speech by Adolf Hitler to introduce a discussion about the “cosmopolitan elite”.

Letschert initially said she was unable to intervene because the public broadcasting service NPO had not asked her to withdraw ON’s licence.

But last week the media regulator CvdM said in a letter to the minister that the broadcaster had failed to comply with its legal obligations, clearing the way for Letschert to take ON off the air.

More than two-thirds of MPs want the publicly funded channel to be removed in the wake of the latest controversy, including all three coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD, RTL Nieuws reported. Parliament is due to debate its future later this month.

ON’s editor-in-chief Joost Niemöller stepped down a week ago because of a ”difference of view about the editorial direction and recent programming”, according to a statement by Vlemmix.

Niemöller was one of the panellists on the show that sparked the row, after he said he agreed with “certain things of Hitler’s” but condemned the Nazi leader’s anti-Semitism.

Vlemmix has said the broadcaster will continue its “fight for survival” and accused the media regulator of overlooking improvements made over the past year.

item.title: Dutch flying car finally cleared for take-off by 2028
item.description:
Dutch flying car finally cleared for take-off by 2028

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch flying car maker PAL-V has been given the go-ahead to start building something that could be in the skies in 2028.

The European aviation safety agency EASA gave the company, based in Noord-Brabant, a production licence, meaning it now has every permit it needs to begin building. It first began designing flying cars 20 years ago.

“Now that EASA approval is in, we will really start producing the first cars soon,” chief executive Robert Dingemanse told broadcaster NOS. “We then have to test them again to show once more that we meet all the guidelines. That takes about a year and a half.”

PAL-V’s models have faced repeated promises and delays in the past – its first car was cleared in 2020 and it said its first commercial model would follow in 2021, which was then postponed to 2025 and then 2026.

The Liberty, which folds its rotor blades away to drive on the road, costs between €299,000 and €499,000. The first 250 are already sold, NOS reported, and the company has stopped taking orders because it can only build 100 per year.

Around half the buyers are fire brigades, police forces and the military, Dingemanse said. The rest are specialists who need to get somewhere fast, plus a handful of wealthy private owners. Apart from the Dutch fire brigade, almost all of them are foreign.

Don’t expect one over your street
The bad news for anyone dreaming of skipping national traffic jams is that the flying car is likely going nowhere in the Netherlands for regular people, no matter how rich you are.

It has to follow the same rules as any aircraft, and can only take off and land at around 20 small airstrips nationwide. “You can’t just fly anywhere,” Delft University aviation professor Jacco Hoekstra told NOS. “And Dutch airspace is pretty full.”

Aviation expert Joris Melkert said the Netherlands has a perfectly good road network, and that unlike a country like Norway, where getting across a fjord in a hurry can be impossible, “a flying car is not crucial here.”

item.title: Van de Zandschulp reaches US Open quarter-finals for second time
item.description:
Van de Zandschulp reaches US Open quarter-finals for second time

September 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch number one tennis player Botic van de Zandschulp has reached the quarter-finals of the US Open after winning a five-hour marathon against Frenchman Arthur Gea.

The 30-year-old came back from two sets down to win the third and fourth sets on a tie-break before clinching the final set 6-4 in a match that swung back and forth.

Van de Zandschulp was warned by the umpire at one point for smashing a ball out of the stadium in frustration, but regained his composure as he wore down Gea, who only got into the tournament as a lucky loser.

“I’ve had some tough years, but since this year things have gone better,” he said afterwards. “I still need to let it sink in, but tomorrow I’ll probably wake up feeling good.”

Gea took the first set 6-3 after Van de Zandschulp failed to convert two break points at 3-3, while in the second set the Dutchman surrendered a 4-1 lead before losing the tie-break to love.

Van de Zandschulp was on the point of going out in straight sets when Gea served for the match in the third-set tie-break.

But the Dutchman won the point and went on to take the fourth set, also on a tie-break, before making the decisive break at 3-3 in the decider. He served out the match to wrap up the win in five hours, 13 minutes.

His reward is a daunting quarter-final against the top seed, Alexander Zverev, after the German beat Italy’s Luciano Darderi in straight sets. Zverev is aiming for his second Grand Slam title after winning the French Open in June and reaching the final of Wimbledon.
